Design review: How the eufyMake E1 UV printer inspired the return of the Design Week Awards

Textured 2.5D UV printing has traditionally been the preserve of high-end print shops. We put eufyMake’s desktop E1 to the test to see what it offers small studios – and accidentally solved our biggest awards headache in the process.

David Coveney
12 November, 2026 Comments
Listen to audio version of this article
0:00 / 0:00 Instaread
Sponsored by

We get a fairly steady stream of manufacturers asking us to review their products. Our rule is simple: if a product offers genuine creative or commercial potential to our readership, we’ll cover it.

In this case, we’re looking at the eufyMake E1 (affiliate link) – a desktop UV printer that produces textured, “2.5D” prints. Textured UV output itself is nothing new, but until now it has mostly lived on costly industrial machines in specialist print shops, well beyond the budget of a small studio.

The surprise of this test was how much the team took to the machine – enough that it finally pushed Design Week into relaunching its awards.

Unpacking and set-up

The E1 arrived while the author was away; within a week colleagues had set it up and printed on phone cases, an old camera, a fridge magnet and dice. Apart from needing yet another online account, setup is easy – a custom phone case takes under an hour.

From test prints to trophy concepts

A little ink lets you print on most surfaces, and a first test on thin plywood came out very well.

Relaunching the awards had always looked too risky, mainly the fear of spending £15k on trophies up front. One evening he wondered if the E1 could print them, stayed late working up a concept with AI, and was impressed by the first test.

His family liked the result, along with a custom phone case and a photo fridge magnet. Further tests showed black acrylic sheet warps in the heat and shifts on the mat.

Choose your substrates and get used to them

Material choice matters commercially: his cheap case has survived two months of daily use, but a failed print on a customer’s phone could ruin it, so merchandise printers use damage waivers or stick to cases.

Shops that make money from UV printers usually keep to well-tested items – one prints team members onto hockey pucks, baseballs and small footballs. On the E1’s flatbed a ball must fit under the head (60mm diameter with camera alignment, 100mm with manual alignment), and eufyMake recommends no more than a 2mm drop from the highest point. On that basis a 20mm logo needs a ball of at least 52mm: baseballs (73mm) allow about 24mm and 100mm mini footballs about 28mm, while golf balls (42.7mm) are borderline at around 18mm.

Each print starts with a UV-cured white layer, which also forms the texture, before colour goes on. Wood needs only one white layer and was among the easiest materials – one concept award was even stolen at an event.

The textured wood pieces were very popular. He adapted a painting by local artist Matt Nightingale into a lightbulb shape, let the software’s AI build a depth map to recreate the brushstrokes, and used the result to discuss an original awards artwork with Matt.

The software – and the rotary reality check

Software now separates good machines from bad. The E1 runs through eufyMake Studio and has a small enclosed bed that limits the smell, plus a large bed with a 330mm x 420mm print area.

A camera locates multiple items on the bed, such as dice or A5 boards, for batch printing, with objects up to 60mm tall (130mm with manual alignment). Round items need the rotary attachment: ink peeled off a steel bottle without primer, while a Pepsi Max can worked well but needed many costly white layers.

Rotary jobs are also slow, because every can or bottle has to be loaded and set up individually, unlike a batch of pucks on the flatbed.

What really is 2.5D printing?

The moving bed enables 2.5D output. Full 3D is possible on some high-end UV printers, but the resin inks must form tiny, thin drops for detail, so overhangs can’t be printed.

Texture can reach 5mm, enough for convincing oil-paint brushstrokes, with AI estimating depth from flat images. Depth maps can also come from 3D tools such as ZBrush.

Maintenance, consumables and costs

Like inkjets, these printers need regular care: the £549 print head is replaced about every eight months, pads and wipes roughly quarterly, with a short monthly clean.

A fully covered textured A4 can use £7 to £13 of ink, a flat one 70p to £2.50; at 1,000 prints a year he budgets an extra £4 per A4 for the machine and upkeep. Head-moistening also uses ink, so occasional users pay more per print.

The verdict

At around £1,599 to £2,149, the E1 makes textured UV printing affordable for small studios, though buyers should allow for the smell, primer wipes, maintenance and slow rotary jobs.

On proven flat materials such as wood, coasters and phone cases the results are excellent – including the studio’s own awards trophies.

eufyMake E1 – Key Specifications

  • Max Print Area: 330mm x 420mm (Standard Bed)
  • Max Texture Height: Up to 5mm (Amass3D™ technology)
  • Max Object Thickness: 60mm (Auto-alignment) – up to 130mm (Manual)
  • Max Surface Drop (Curved Items): 2mm recommended throw distance
  • Print Resolution: Up to 1440 DPI
  • Ink System: 6-channel (CMYK + White + Gloss)
  • Software: eufyMake Studio (macOS / Windows / iOS / Android)
  • RRP: From £1,599 (Basic Bundle) – £2,149 standard (based on current deals)
  • Affiliate link: Support Design Week using this link

For the studio, then, the review unit did more than fill a test slot: it gave the team a practical, in-house way to make trophies and to move ahead with the awards relaunch.
